summary:
Malacca is one of the thirteen states of Malaysia and stands under the Malaysian national framework. Sections 377A and 377B of the Federal Penal Code 1936 criminalise same-sex sexual activity with a maximum penalty of twenty years' imprisonment and whipping, and section 377D, covering outrages on decency and gross indecency, is drafted in terms that can be used to target transgender people. A non-Muslim, non-citizen visitor in Malacca is exposed to the federal Penal Code alone; the parallel Sharia enactments that criminalise cross-dressing and gender nonconformity apply only to Muslims.

The Human Dignity Trust Malaysia country profile, last updated in 2024, records evidence of these provisions being enforced in recent years and a broader crackdown on the LGBT community following the 2018 election. It also documents a high-profile 2021 case in which a prominent transgender woman fled the country after threats of arrest.

An August 2022 report by Human Rights Watch with Justice for Sisters describes government-sponsored discrimination against LGBT people across Malaysia. The report details conversion and rehabilitation programmes and officials shutting down events, and concludes that pervasive antipathy toward sexual and gender diversity shapes law enforcement, judicial outcomes, family behaviour and public discourse.

Consistent reports of discrimination and violence are recorded, with transgender people particularly vulnerable to physical and verbal abuse. Both sources are national in scope and give no enforcement breakdown for Malacca specifically.
tangentialFactors:
The regulatory picture for a visitor is set nationally rather than locally: the sources treat Malaysian law as a single regime, so conduct that draws attention in Kuala Lumpur or Selangor carries the same exposure in Malacca. Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters identify event shutdowns and conversion or rehabilitation programmes as standing instruments of that regime, meaning visibility at social venues can trigger official action irrespective of any arrest under the Penal Code.

The 2021 flight of a prominent transgender woman following threats of arrest indicates that exposure can materialise as pressure to leave rather than as a completed prosecution. The trajectory of the crackdown since the 2018 election has been toward broader and more public action, which raises the baseline risk for a visibly gender-nonconforming traveller compared with earlier periods.
localsOnly:
Residents of Malacca who are Muslim fall under both the Federal Penal Code and the state Sharia enactment, which criminalises cross-dressing and male-to-female presentation; state religious authorities carry out enforcement and may impose penalties including imprisonment, fines and caning under the wider Malaysian pattern.

Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters document conversion and rehabilitation programmes applied to LGBT Malaysians, alongside the shutdown of events and pervasive discrimination in family and institutional settings. Transgender residents are recorded as particularly exposed to physical and verbal abuse, with limited practical recourse where the state itself is a source of the discrimination.

The 2021 case of a prominent transgender woman who left the country under threat of arrest is documented as a Selangor matter but reflects conditions that apply to residents of every Malaysian state, Malacca included.
outOfScopeNotes:
Neither source supplies enforcement data specific to Malacca, so the frequency and manner of local enforcement under sections 377A, 377B and 377D, and any recent operations by the Malacca state religious authority against transgender residents, remain unresolved on this inventory.

The Human Dignity Trust profile was last updated in 2024 and the Human Rights Watch report is dated August 2022; developments after those dates are not covered here and cannot be confirmed from these sources.

No visa or entry rule specific to transgender visitors appears in this inventory. The question of how gender markers on foreign passports are treated at Malaysian entry points is not sourced and remains unresolved.
